claims.text: Applying an ultra-thin, high-conductivity metal coating to tungsten surfaces reduces electron scattering at W–Cu interfaces.
Reduced interfacial electron scattering enhances electronic coupling between tungsten and copper.
Reducing mismatch at W–Cu interfaces facilitates smoother electron transport.
Improved electron transport increases the electronic contribution to thermal conductivity and thus the composite's overall thermal conductivity.
Relative to an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite, the coated composite will have measurably higher thermal conductivity.
Making the coating ultra-thin minimizes adverse effects on mechanical properties.
The ultra-thin coating limits additional stress concentrations.
Limiting coating-induced stress concentrations helps avoid additional irradiation damage.
The coated W–Cu composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to that of an uncoated control.
The coated W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of an uncoated control.
Fusion-reactor service calls for thermal conductivity, irradiation resistance, and tolerance of temperature variations.
The proposed benefit depends on the coating remaining continuous and defect-free during processing and service.
Significant coating degradation or delamination under thermal cycling or irradiation would prevent the expected benefit.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity enhancement depends on coating thickness, uniformity, and long-term stability.
